as_told.title: Pilot Bud Clem follows a ball of light over Hanford

tellings.quote: During the war, Clarence R. “Bud” Clem was a Lieutenant Junior Grade in the U.S. Naval Reserves, serving as an F6F Hellcat fighter pilot assigned to Air Group 50 aboard the U.S.S. Cowpens CVL-25.
Brown quickly found the object, a bright ball of fire, and took chase. But he could not close [on it], even with water injection that gave a quick boost in speed.
He later sent me his military records which revealed that his fighter squadron was actually at Pasco from January 9 to February 15, 1945, not during March and April, as he had first indicated.
Given the available data, it appears that bona fide UFOs were in fact operating near the Hanford site in early 1945, only months prior to the attacks on Hiroshima and Nagasaki.

plain: In early 1945, months before the first atomic test and the bombing of Japan, glowing balls of light are said to have hovered over Hanford, the plant in Washington state where plutonium for the bomb was made, and fighter planes could not catch them. Michels tells it often, drawing on the researcher Robert Hastings. He describes "luminous balls of light hovering" over the site and "being chased away unsuccessfully by jet fighters", and names a pilot, Bud Clem, sometimes as the man following a ball of light himself. In one telling he ties it to Project Twinkle, which he says was "deleted from the Air Force archives". Hastings' article of August 9, 2015 gives the source. It says Clarence "Bud" Clem was a Navy fighter pilot flying the F6F Hellcat. It says another pilot, Brown, found "a bright ball of fire, and took chase. But he could not close [on it]", even with a boost in speed. Clem's records, Hastings writes, put the squadron nearby "from January 9 to February 15, 1945", not in spring as Clem first recalled. Hastings concludes that "bona fide UFOs were in fact operating near the Hanford site in early 1945". If so, they were watching the bomb before the world knew it existed.
